note: £4,401 came in from the customer's own Harbourline Bank account (28-63-84 21377918) and went out the next day to their own Meadowcroft Building Society savings account (23-94-28 80396743). Both statements are in Finley Kingscombe's name and show the same amount and dates, and the account numbers match the payments. It's 1.6 times declared income, below the 5x policy line, so it's simply savings being moved.
lesson: Money passing through within 48 hours is not a concern when both ends are the customer's own accounts: a statement in the customer's name for the sending account, another for the receiving account, the same amount and dates, and matching account numbers. Close as own account when below 5 times declared income.

note: Five cash top-ups of £820-£965 (£4,385) over 7-16 October. The customer is a self-employed market trader, and the takings book TAK-1425 lists each market day with takings and the cash topped up. Every top-up matches its row to the pound and is below that day's takings. For a sole trader with no till system, the takings book is the business record, and the volume fits the declared self-employment.
lesson: Repeated cash top-ups just under a threshold are explained for a cash-based sole trader when a takings record lists each trading day and the top-up for that day matches to the pound and doesn't exceed the takings. For a sole trader the takings book is the business record. Escalate instead if the customer asks how to avoid checks, or the amounts exceed what the record supports.

note: The £1,230 cash top-up on 16 September matches the bill of sale SAL-333 for the customer's carbon road bike, sold for £1,230 cash to Rowan Stangate on 15 September. The customer's own advert ADV-3418 from 4 September offered the same bike at £1,380 "or near offer", cash on collection, so the sale price and cash payment fit. One-off, small, and the day after the sale.
lesson: A cash top-up above the limit is explained by a one-off private sale when an advert placed beforehand by the customer shows they were selling the item for cash, and a bill of sale for the same item matches the amount and is dated just before the top-up. A sale below the asking price is normal.

note: The £7,605 credit from Everton Services Ltd, referenced "SETTLEMENT AGREEMENT", matches to the pound the settlement letter SET-7789 of 5 September promising £7,605 compensation for loss of office within 14 days; it arrived on 12 September. Other inflows are small top-ups from the customer.

The single £9,334.54 SWIFT payment to Langgate University Medical Center in Beirut matches to the penny the hospital invoice INV-3154 for Quinn Marbrook's coronary bypass surgery, and the payment reference names the patient. The customer explained it as their parent's surgery, and the surname matches. The money went to the hospital itself, as a one-off.
lesson: Same rule as for hospital and university payments abroad: a one-off payment straight to the institution, matching its invoice in payee, amount and patient or student, is explained even in a higher-risk country.

note: Twelve friends each paid £345 for a group trip to Lisbon. Booking BKG-1790, dated 27 July before any money came in, lists 13 travellers at £345 each (£4,485), due by 21 August to Penworth Travel Ltd, with the customer as lead traveller. Every payer is named on it, and on 21 August exactly £4,485 went to Penworth Travel Ltd with reference "BOOKING TR74014".
lesson: A group collection is fully evidenced when every payer appears on the booking, each pays the per-person price, and the total goes to the merchant named on the booking, with the booking reference, by the due date.

note: The list hit is on address only: entry EM-L41674 is Bailey Aldden (born 1969), who ran Radford Imports Ltd from Unit 4B, Radmore Works. The payee, Calwick Print Studio Ltd, is at Unit 4A, and its register REG-4804 shows director and owner Reese Sandhurst, born September 1996. Different unit, company and person. The £260 matches the course booking RCT-6687 and the "Screen printing course" reference.
lesson: A watch-list match on address only is a different party when the payee is at a different unit of the same building and its register shows different directors and owners from the listed subject. A shared building or business park isn't a link.

note: £1,790 came in from Whithurst Lettings Ltd as "DEPOSIT RETURN", matching the deposit return letter LET-8484 of 18 August, and the customer added £885 of their own money. The next day £2,525 went to Elmridge Homes Ltd as "HOLDING DEPOSIT", matching Elmridge's receipt LET-6574 for the new flat. The old tenancy deposit came back and was used for the new one.

After 326 days without activity, £19,051.99 arrived from Cranden Life Assurance plc with reference "CLAIM 50453". It matches to the penny the insurer's letter INS-5795 of 5 September, addressed to Rowan Corcote, accepting a critical illness claim. Nothing has left the account since, and the only contact on file is a routine address check, so there are no takeover signs.
lesson: A payout from a regulated insurer into a dormant account is explained when the reference and amount match the insurer's letter to the customer and nothing suspicious follows (no new payees, no quick outflows).

note: A retail assistant on £1,250 a month received about £12,000 from eight individuals on 2-3 September, with mixed references ("loan", "thanks", "car parts", "rent deposit", "tickets"), and 91% went out within 48 hours, with a transfer to Coinvale Exchange held for checks. Two sending banks (RPT-3315, RPT-9335) report their customers were scammed. In chat CHT-392 the customer describes a remote "payments assistant" job forwarding clients' money to a crypto account for an 8% cut, found on social media. Device export DEV-1756 shows logins from the UK and Nigeria.
lesson: Fraud reports from sending banks, a customer describing a job receiving and forwarding other people's money for a cut, crypto outflows and logins from abroad on a new device are each signs of a mule account. Any one with fast pass-through means escalate, never RFI.

note: £1,880 came in from Calford Lettings Ltd as "DEPOSIT RETURN", the customer added £865, and the next day £2,745 went to Cranfield Homes Ltd as "HOLDING DEPOSIT". That looks like an old tenancy deposit being reused for a new flat, a low-risk pattern, but unlike similar cases there's no deposit return letter or holding deposit receipt on file. Ask for both.
lesson: A returned tenancy deposit reused for a new holding deposit is low risk, but without the letting agents' letters it isn't evidenced. Send an RFI for the deposit return letter and the holding deposit receipt. Close when both match the amounts and payees.

note: £12,608 arrived from Bromdale Logistics Ltd with reference "SETTLEMENT AGREEMENT", about four months of the customer's declared income. There's no settlement letter or agreement on file to confirm what it is or that the customer is entitled to it. Ask for the signed settlement agreement.

£14,404.85 came from the customer's own Kestrel Mutual account (30-20-10 60672010), reference "FROM SAVINGS", and statement STM-6553 in Remy Gargate's name shows the same transfer on 12 October. The money is the customer's own, but it takes 30-day receipts to 6.3 times declared income, above the 5x policy line, so the policy requires an RFI for an updated expected income.
lesson: Proven own-account transfers still need an RFI for an updated profile when they take activity to 5 times declared income or more. This is a policy rule, not a suspicion.

note: Thirteen people each paid £185 (£2,405), all with "Lake Garda" or "Trip" references, and on 7 October £2,590 went to Millridge Travel Ltd with reference "BOOKING TR28733". It looks like a group trip the customer is organising, but there's no booking confirmation on file to show the payers, per-person price or total. Ask for the booking confirmation.
lesson: Same as for any group collection: consistent references and a payment to a travel company point to a genuine group booking, but without the booking on file send an RFI for it rather than closing.

note: The £2,200 payment on 17 August went to Hartmere Consulting Ltd, matching invoice INV-2735 for a coaching course. But list entry EM-L23243 is Robin Stanholt (born May 1977), under unresolved investigation, "do not deal with this person or companies they control". The register shows Robin resigned as director on 16 August, but the control register PSC-3067 shows he still owned 60% of the company until 19 August. On the payment date the listed person controlled the payee.
lesson: On a watch-list match against a company officer, check who controlled the company on the payment date, not just today. Look at both the directors' list and the ownership (significant control) register, with appointment, resignation and ceased dates. If the listed person was a director or major owner when the payment was made, escalate as a listed party, even if they resigned around that time and the invoice looks genuine.

note: Seven cash top-ups of £905-£985 (£6,625) at five locations on 17-18 October, by a software developer on £1,700 a month, and 94% left within 48 hours. Staff note NTE-1749: while depositing £930 the customer asked whether top-ups at different shops are added together and whether staying under £1,000 avoids ID checks.

£20,017 arrived from Norford Trading Ltd as "CONSULTANCY", but register REG-4248 shows the company was dissolved on 19 September 2025. The customer told us in CHT-6308 it's "a loan from a friend to help with bills", yet within a day £18,015.30 went out in three identical £6,005.10 payments to three individuals. The reference, explanation and outflows all contradict each other.
lesson: A payer company that is dissolved, an explanation that contradicts the payment reference, and money split equally to several individuals straight away are each grounds to escalate. Don't send an RFI after the customer has already given a contradicted explanation.

note: The £925 payment to "Sidney Cranstead" for "Garden landscaping" matched list entry EM-L49319 on name only; the listed person's relationship was exited in 2024 after unexplained third-party payments. Nothing on file identifies the payee (no invoice, business details, address or date of birth), so we can't tell. Ask for the landscaper's invoice and business details.
lesson: A name-only watch-list match with nothing on file about the payee is an RFI for counterparty details, not a close and not an escalation.

note: Three individuals sent the customer £21,493.68 on 10-12 September, each referenced "transfer", and within days four identical £4,567.41 SWIFT payments went to four different individuals in Haiti, referenced "family support". Haiti is higher risk and not declared, none of the recipients share the customer's surname, and the money came from third parties rather than the customer's £2,800 salary. The only explanation is a one-line chat.
lesson: Money from several third parties sent straight on in identical amounts to several individuals in a higher-risk country is not family support from the customer's own money. Escalate as a higher-risk corridor, whatever the stated reference.

note: After 397 days without activity, £8,550 came in from the customer's own Wexmoor Bank account (78-53-76 37324610), and statement STM-731 in Charlie Corwell's name shows the same transfer on 9 August. The day before, the customer's identity was re-verified with a live selfie on the device already registered (RVF-329), and they explained they'd been working in Dubai for a year. At 4.5 times declared income it's below the 5x line. The only spending since is a £79 supermarket payment.

Money mule: 8 unrelated payers 4-8 Aug forwarded to Coinvale Exchange Ltd plus ATM cash; customer keeps 8% for an online 'payments assistant' job (CHT-4160); APP scam reports RPT-1763, RPT-8844; new device with UK/Nigeria logins (DEV-3165). Review EM-R417436 covers only a holiday booking

Listed Charlie Talton (EM-L82249, b. Jan 1978) controlled payee Langwell Consulting Ltd on payment date 12 Oct: 60% PSC until 14 Oct (PSC-9507), resigned as director only 11 Oct (REG-9684). Invoice INV-3614 matches £3,400 but does not cure control by listed party

7 cash top-ups £915-£985 at 5 outlets on 9-10 Oct (£6,690), customer asked outlet staff about keeping top-ups under £1,000 to avoid ID (NTE-911); £6,355.50 sent on to Coinvale Exchange Ltd same day (EM-T854329554)

£21.6k in 2-4 Sep from 3 unrelated payers (Sam Calden, Riley Elmstead, Jordan Cranbrook), out 5-7 Sep as 4 identical USD 6,147.71 SWIFTs to 4 different people in Lebanon (undeclared); only explanation vague 'family' (CHT-1088), no docs. ESC_PASS_THROUGH also fits

One-off bike sale: advert ADV-3398 (28 Jul, carbon road bike £2,200 ono, cash on collection, seller Max Fernhurst) and sale receipt SAL-8950 (8 Aug, £2,010 cash from Logan Cranley) match the £2,010 cash top-up on 9 Aug (EM-T680018892)

Dormant 345 days; reactivated by £8,731.07 from 'Peyton Radstead' account 85-64-99 36624801 ref SAVINGS (EM-T576748841), then only a £79 card spend. No document shows customer holds that account, so own-account close not allowed; ask for a statement of it / source of the savings

£4,550 in from Calder Savings Bank 12-28-21 91412434 on 13 Aug and out to Brightwater Bank 10-59-64 57936742 on 14 Aug; statements STM-9167 and STM-3360 show both held by Kit Bramdale with matching amounts/dates; 1.75x income, below the 5x RFI threshold
